leads.name: Blackjack Oak, City of Dallas park (Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 6436)
leads.reason: County-champion-caliber blackjack oak from the Texas Big Tree Registry ArcGIS layer (circumference 121 in / 307 cm, height 61 ft, spread 81 ft, measured 2025-09-03, org City of Dallas, public). Coordinates 32.76527778, -96.75583333 but no named park identified this pass (reverse search pointed vaguely at the Oak Cliff / Lake Cliff / South Dallas area, no confident match). No second independent source found. Needs: which park, and a corroborating source, before it can verify. OWNER per the registry: City of Dallas. That field is what actually answers hard rule 10, better than any flag: a city parks department, a university campus, a county precinct or a churchyard is a yes, and the access line still has to say honestly what a visitor meets.
leads.deepen_pass_2026-09-12: Re-chased. The coordinate reverse-geocodes to 3915 Roberts Avenue, 75215, a residential address, with Oakland Cemetery and Leo V. Chaney Park both within about 250m. Oakland Cemetery's own history page confirms blackjack oak was among the original tree cover on that ground, which supports a cemetery placement in principle but names no specific champion specimen. No source ties the registry point to either the cemetery or the park by name. Per the file's own 2026-08-20 note, resolving this by picking the nearer park is the bridge-claim error and is refused. Still unplaceable; needs a photo, a city forestry record, or someone standing there.

leads.name: Oriental Arborvitae, Cox Cemetery (Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 58)
leads.reason: Texas STATE CHAMPION per the registry (circumference 85 in / 216 cm, height 42 ft, measured 2002-05-15) at Cox Cemetery near White Rock Lake (32.84135, -96.73135), a public pioneer cemetery (400+ marked graves, oldest stone 1848). Register is the only source found; a web search turned up plenty on the cemetery itself but nothing on this specific tree. Also a judgement call: an ornamental non-native cemetery arborvitae may read as a curiosity rather than an epic, walk-worthy tree even as a state champion. Needs a second source and a look at whether it clears the remarkable bar. OWNER per the registry: Cox Cemetery. That field is what actually answers hard rule 10, better than any flag: a city parks department, a university campus, a county precinct or a churchyard is a yes, and the access line still has to say honestly what a visitor meets.
leads.deepen_pass_2026-09-12: Searched again specifically for the tree (not just the cemetery). Still nothing beyond the registry: plenty on Cox Cemetery's pioneer graves and its historical marker, nothing naming this arborvitae. The measurement is also 24 years stale (2002) with no re-check on file. Stays a lead; the champion-species designation alone is not the two-source bar.

Stays a lead.

blocked.name: Champion Black Willow, White Rock Lake / East Lawther Drive
blocked.reason: DEAD. Was the Texas state champion black willow (circumference 265 in, added to the registry 2011) near East Lawther Drive east of White Rock Lake. Accidentally cut down by a city contractor stump-grinding crew in early Feb 2015 (NBC5, CultureMap Dallas, D Magazine, CBS News all covered it). Another black willow has since taken the state champion title elsewhere in Texas, not confirmed to be in Dallas. Never ship this entry.

blocked.name: Gateway Park Comanche Marker Tree
blocked.reason: DEAD. Per TxHTC (https://txhtc.org/trees/gateway-park-comanche-marker-tree/), officially recognized by the Comanche Tribal Government in 1997, but the tree was already in poor health from surrounding development and was lost in the Memorial Day storm of 25 May 1998. Page itself is headed 'Deceased 1998'. Confirmed again 2026-09-12 while researching the separate Storytelling Place tree (Texas Parks & Wildlife magazine, Nov 2006, names this Gateway Park pecan specifically as the one destroyed in the storm, distinct from the Storytelling Place site in Devon-Anderson Park). Never ship.

blocked.name: Texas Discovery Gardens Cottonwood, Fair Park
blocked.reason: DEAD/REMOVED. Per TxHTC (https://txhtc.org/trees/texas-discovery-gardens-cottonwood/ and /texas-discovery-gardens-cottonwood-3/), declared historic in 2003 after witnessing roughly 50 State Fairs, but it later became a safety hazard (sloughing bark and branches) and was removed by Preservation Tree Services; two sections were kept and carved into sculptures now displayed at the Natural Learning Center. blocked.name: Cedrus deodara, Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 337
sources: Texas Big Tree Registry, Texas A&M Forest Service (texasforestinfo.tamu.edu/BigTreeRegistry). Non-commercial licence: usable as a lead and verification source, never imported. See OPEN_DATA_SURVEY.md.
blocked.why_blocked: PRIVATE LAND. The Texas Big Tree Registry's PublicOrPrivate flag is 0 on this tree, and the flag is not the undocumented mystery an earlier pass took it for: across all 660 swept trees, flag 1 belongs to Big Bend and Guadalupe Mountains National Parks, Sam Houston National Forest, state natural areas and TxDOT districts, while flag 0 belongs to Big Tree Ranch, X-Arrow Ranch, Little Sandy Hunting & Fishing Club and similar. It means what it says. The registry also sets Display 0 on almost all of them, so it withholds these locations from its own public map, and hard rule 10 is absolute about not undoing that: the coordinates only reached us because the backend returns what the front end hides. Never ship unless a source shows the site is genuinely open to visitors.

notes.note: Swept from the corrected Texas Big Tree Registry pull (scripts/texas_big_trees.py). Circumference is INCHES: an earlier Houston pass read it as centimetres and concluded the state was thin. Coordinates decide which city a tree belongs to, never CountyName.

PublicOrPrivate decoded from the data itself: flag 1 is national parks, national forests, state natural areas and TxDOT; flag 0 is ranches and hunting clubs. Flag 0 trees moved to blocked under hard rule 10, since the registry also hides them from its own public map and their coordinates only reached us because the backend returns what the front end withholds. OrganizationName names the owner and is the field a verify pass should lead with.

The blackjack oak (TreeID 6436, 307 cm, City of Dallas, measured September 2025) was chased again and is still not placeable. Reverse geocoding puts 32.76528,-96.75583 at 3915 Roberts Avenue, 75215, a house number on a residential street, with Oakland Cemetery and Leo V. Cheney Park both within 250 metres. Either the coordinate carries about a hundred metres of error and the tree is in one of those, or it stands on a residential lot the city happens to own. Do NOT resolve this by choosing the nearer park: 'there is a park 200 metres away, therefore the tree is in the park' is the bridge claim that put Baarn's pin sixty metres from the tree it described. What settles it is a photograph, a city park tree inventory, or somebody standing there.

Deepen pass on all 14 open leads plus the four Comanche marker-tree candidates. One verified: the Storytelling Place Red Oak at Devon-Anderson Park (Great Trinity Forest / White Rock Heritage District), a sacred Comanche storytelling site with an ancient red oak regrowing from an old stump, corroborated by TxHTC and an independent trail blog; delivered to data/research/dallas-verified.json as dal_009, flagged (no recent dated sighting). Removed from this file's leads: that entry (now verified) and the Quercus stellata TreeID 2356 entry, which was a stale duplicate of the already-published dal_003 (W.W. Glover Cemetery Post Oak, same coordinate and girth). Four leads (Salix nigra 1134, Fraxinus pennsylvanica 1214, Quercus shumardii 221, Acer negundo 910) confirmed as Tarrant County / Fort Worth-Grapevine trees, 27-32 km out: correctly excluded from Dallas, not re-litigated. Two more leads confirmed out of Dallas's boundary by reverse geocoding: the Coppell bur oak (TreeID 915, 28.7 km, in Coppell) and a Fraxinus pennsylvanica (TreeID 7433, 22.4 km, in Lancaster). Two small-species leads (Eysenhardtia texana TreeID 2361, Ungnadia speciosa TreeID 2336) turned out to share one coordinate in Plano, Collin County, 30.0 km out, likely one private collection: also out of scope. The Ilex vomitoria lead (TreeID 145) reverse-geocodes to an ordinary residential street in Oak Lawn with no park match and a modest girth; the Cox Cemetery Oriental Arborvitae (TreeID 58) and Dallas Arboretum Chalk Maple (TreeID 1253) still lack any second source or particular reason to single them out. All four remaining Comanche marker-tree candidates in Dallas proper are now accounted for: three confirmed dead (already blocked) and the fourth (Storytelling Place) verified alive and shipped. No candidate on this list needs Dallas taken from zero: the register-lead route is exhausted for now, and any further Dallas growth should come from a from-zero web pass (city parks, churchyards, cemeteries not yet searched) rather than more registry leads, since the registry's Dallas-area entries are now all resolved one way or another.
